HONG KONG — Eric Wu, a 37-year-old construction worker, has spent his entire adult life building and climbing bamboo scaffolding as high as 50 floors above the ground.
But on Monday morning, he used his talents to pursue a different goal — lashing together two-inch-thick bamboo poles in an elaborate lattice that he designed to protect an encampment of pro-democracy student protesters here. The lattice was a yard high, about 20 feet wide and 30 feet deep, and blocked a road just a block from the
Hong Kong
police headquarters.
He paused occasionally from expertly lashing together 12-foot-long poles with strips of black plastic to give instructions to student protesters, who were more clumsily trying to tie poles together using long lengths of clear plastic wrapping. He talked about how he thought democracy would create a better Hong Kong, but also gave an economic reason for his presence at the demonstration: “Times are tough, there are no jobs in construction.”
Protesters added more bamboo-pole lattices to their barricades through Monday evening, and were sawing off the ends of some of the longer poles to give them long, sharp points. If the protesters wield the poles as pikes, they could make it considerably more dangerous for police or others to try to disperse and remove them.
At his daily afternoon news conference on Monday, Hui Chun-tak, the chief police spokesman, labeled all further construction of barricades as “illegal and highly irresponsible,” though he did not single out bamboo barricades in particular.
Mr. Wu’s labors brought together one of
China
’s oldest traditions — bamboo scaffolding — with Hong Kong’s widespread aspirations for democracy, particularly among the young, and a dissatisfaction with the local economy among blue-collar workers.
Bamboo scaffolding is an ancient building technique in China, in use for more than 1,000 years. While mainland China has curtailed its use for buildings more than six stories tall for safety reasons, it remains popular in Hong Kong.
Generations of construction workers here have learned through an elaborate apprenticeship system the techniques of lashing bamboo together. Construction executives and engineers say that bamboo offers a sturdy yet flexible alternative to steel, particularly in a coastal environment where strong winds and typhoons can blow in off the South China Sea.
Bamboo is still popular in Hong Kong because the poles are one-sixth the price and one-third the weight of steel poles, and they can be erected in half the time of steel scaffolding, said Flord So, the chairman of the Hong Kong and Kowloon Scaffolders General Merchant Association, a trade group. Bamboo poles are somewhat more likely to break, including in storms, but inflict far less damage when they fall than do steel poles, he added.
Mr. Wu began creating his bamboo barrier after the police, in a series of raids on protest encampments Monday, carted off many of the barriers of steel or super-hardened plastic that the students had been using. Most of these barriers actually belonged to the police, but the students had commandeered them when the police largely withdrew from the city center on Sept. 29.

Blue-collar workers like Mr. Wu, often unemployed and disaffected by the high cost of living in Hong Kong, have joined the protesters in significant numbers, although students appear to make up the largest share of protesters.
The overall unemployment rate in Hong Kong has stayed steady for the last several years at around 3.3 percent. But the broad rate disguises pockets of unemployment among the young and less educated. Unemployment has been a particular problem among construction workers, as builders have imported inexpensive prefabricated sections of buildings from factories in mainland China, reducing the need for labor in Hong Kong.
Sam Tse, a 54-year-old electrician, came to the demonstrations on Monday afternoon for the first time to show support for the protesters and their calls for democracy. He said that he lived in public housing and despaired of earning enough to buy his own home in Hong Kong, where studio apartments measuring just 177 square feet and in an outlying area went on sale this summer for $250,000.
“It was tough to make a living before, but if you worked hard, you could move up — now, even if you work hard, you can’t move ahead,” Mr. Tse complained.
Mr. Wu and Mr. Tse declined to give their full Chinese names, fearing that could make it easier for the police to track them down if the protests triggered a broader crackdown.
After Mr. Wu and the students finished the construction of their bamboo lattice, Mr. Wu headed to another barricade that students were reinforcing with scavenged sheets of plywood. Mr. Wu studied their efforts, and began barking instructions.
“If we can just find some nails,” he said, “this barrier will be very sturdy.”

Developing technology is one thing; democratizing it is another. The latter involves finding the innovation that opens the door to widespread adoption with usefulness and usability.
In the personal computer era, it was the spreadsheet that transformed a hobbyists’ plaything into a must-have machine in corporate America. In mobile computing, it was Apple’s iPhone that brought the smartphone to the masses, establishing a new model for the gadgets as both smart and easy to use. In the era of big data, start-ups and big companies are in hot pursuit of a similar breakthrough, a vehicle to bring modern data analysis and prediction to the rank and file of business.
IBM thinks it has an answer, called Watson Analytics, which it announced on Tuesday. The offering is a software service, delivered over the cloud. As its name suggests, Watson Analytics is a result of a collaboration between teams from IBM’s data analysis group and its Watson unit, which has been
built into a business
in the three years since Watson beat human champions in the question-and-answer game “Jeopardy.”
The combined team of data scientists, developers and designers has been working on the project for a year. Its ambitious goal, according to Alistair Rennie, general manager of IBM Business Analytics, is to take a big step toward “getting analytics in the hands of every business user, which is a real challenge.”
IBM has shown an early working version of Watson Analytics to a handful of customers and industry analysts, letting them try it out, and they are generally impressed. It combines basics of data handling with the Watson technologies of natural-language processing and machine learning. A result, they say, is that a business person, who is not a statistician or data scientist, can type in questions to probe corporate data. Examples: “What high-value customers am I most likely to close sales with in the next 30 days?” and “Which benefits drive employee retention the most?”
Watson Analytics, they say, may respond with answers ranked by probabilities or with suggestions. The suggestions can begin a sort of dialogue, recommendations to improve the data used or add other sources. It can, for example, rate the quality of the data probed by an initial inquiry. More reliable predictions, the Watson software might say, would result from cleaning the data or including other sources, like local weather or traffic flows, for retail sales predictions, for example.
Click a button, and Watson Analytics, will do that. “It does a lot automatically, with behind-the-scenes intelligence,” said Dan Vesset, an analyst at IDC.
The IBM tool, Mr. Vesset said, can reply in text answers in addition to traditional visual representations of data like charts and graphs. The natural-language capability, he noted, goes beyond the visualization offerings by companies like Tableau, Qlik and SAS Institute.
A brisk demonstration running through a selection of cases does not mean the product will be a winner in the broad corporate market. Still, a couple of the veteran technology managers who have tried out Watson Analytics say it could be a significant advance. Richard Wiedenbeck, chief information officer of Ameritas, a life insurance and financial services company in Lincoln, Neb., said that he was “cautiously optimistic” that Watson Analytics could deliver on its promise, based on what he had seen so far.
“It looks like IBM has leapfrogged what others have done,” Mr. Wiedenbeck said. “It feels like the iPhone of analytics to me.”
Aaron Walz is director of the Business Intelligence Competency Center at Purdue, which applies data analysis tools to everything from classroom scheduling to identifying factors correlated with on-time graduation rates. The field of data tools, Mr. Walz said, has “really struggled with adoption,” mainly because the technology has been too difficult for nonexperts to use.
To be won over, Mr. Walz said he would have to see how Watson Analytics works in day-to-day use. But, he added, “it looks quite compelling.”

For an American growing up today, it can be difficult to imagine that the United States once dominated the men’s professional tennis circuit. “It would be nice if America actually had a famous tennis player,” said Noah Rubin, an 18-year-old who will make his first appearance in the United­ States Open this week. In 2003, the last year an American man won a Grand Slam tournament — Andy Roddick at the U.S. Open — Rubin was just starting second grade on Long Island. “Any of my friends who aren’t huge tennis fans have barely heard of Andy Roddick,” he said the other day at the club where he trains on Randalls Island. “They’re like, ‘Wasn’t he a male model?’ ” (Close, Rubin’s father said: Roddick is married to a model, Brooklyn Decker.)
In May 1984, as
Christopher Clarey of The New York Times recently noted
, six of the world’s Top 10 were American, as were 24 of the Top 50. A decade later, there were four in the Top 10 and 11 in the Top 50. Last May, there was only one American in the Top 50, and that was the lumbering 29-year-old journeyman John Isner, who has never made it past the quarterfinals of a major tournament. Spain, meanwhile, has 10 players in the Top 50; France has seven.
Rubin is one of a class of prospects being cultivated in the hope of someday putting the U.S. back on top. On July 6, he won the boys’ singles title at Wimbledon by beating Stefan Kozlov of Pembroke Pines, Fla., his friend and sometime doubles partner, in the final. (He followed that by winning the U.S.T.A. national championship for boys 18 and under this month in Kalamazoo, Mich., which gave him entry to the men’s draw of the U.S. Open.) Rubin arrived at Wimbledon as a qualifier and had to play his way into the main junior draw by winning two preliminary rounds. Still, with his foot speed, his ability to control play with both his forehand and backhand and his acuity as a counterpuncher, he defeated a series of more powerful players. In the third round, he beat the seventh-seeded Francis Tiafoe of Maryland, who last December, at 15, won the international Junior Orange Bowl 18-and-unders. In the semifinals, Rubin’s victim was Taylor Harry Fritz, a tall 16-year-old from California with a monstrous serve. Last came the baby-faced — and favored — Kozlov, who is 16.
Lawrence Kleger, who shares coaching duties with Rubin’s father, writes messages to Rubin before each match that he doesn’t attend. He says he found himself delivering three inspirational notes that ended with, “This is another next top junior in America you’re about to beat.” Rubin is only the fourth American champion of junior Wimbledon since 1977 — which, by the way, was the last time two boys from the United States faced off in the final. After Rubin won, Kozlov dug around in his racket bag and pulled out an American flag. Winner and runner-up held it aloft and then took off on a two-man victory lap.
“If it had been anybody other than Stefan, I probably wouldn’t have done it,” Rubin said. “Cumulatively, I’ve probably roomed with Stefan for two months’ worth of overnights, which in his case is a lot of your life.” Rubin added: “It could’ve seemed obnoxious. But every American player has a lot of pressure on them. I figured, why not?”

Patrick McEnroe, a younger brother of John McEnroe and then the U.S. Davis Cup team captain, was appointed the U.S.T.A.’s general manager of player development. His mandate was to remedy what he calls “the situation with the men.” McEnroe says that in the past, there was no need for something like this. “Elite tennis players seemed to be produced in America on their own.” McEnroe supervised a group of training centers for young players and a year-round academy in Florida. With an annual academy budget of about $17 million — financed with revenue from the U.S. Open ­ — the U.S.T.A. invited the most accomplished teenagers in the country to train full time on its new campus in Boca Raton, where they could also complete their high-school degrees without charge. “We’d like to do what Spain has done, creating a wave of good, Top 100 players and having a few great players rise to the top,” McEnroe says. “When you put them all together, they push each other to get there.”
In coaching circles, it’s widely accepted that a push is needed. Some blame technique or tactics for America’s fall: Partly because most Americans don’t grow up playing on clay courts, which yield a slower and higher-bouncing ball, they don’t develop the strokes or strategy suited to adequate “point construction.” Others fault cultural norms, arguing that prospects are poorly taught because American tennis lacks a rigorous system for certifying teaching pros. Still others question whether players should turn pro as teenagers or — as the U.S.T.A. generally urges — play four years of college tennis instead and join the tour around 22. And then there’s the matter of privilege, which means Americans may require a different coaching style. “You can’t really threaten American kids to play their heart out. You have to encourage them, because they always get dessert,” Kleger says. Lending some credence to this theory is the fact that three of the most promising American 16-year-olds — Kozlov, Tiafoe and Michael Mmoh, whom Rubin defeated in Kalamazoo — are all the children of recent immigrants.
All three also enrolled at intensive tennis factories. Kozlov, whose parents left Russia when he was an infant, turned pro at 13 and now trains under the joint supervision of his father, who opened his own tennis academy in Florida, and the U.S.T.A. academy. Tiafoe, whose parents fled war-torn Sierra Leone, is enrolled at a full-time program in Maryland, where his father was part of the construction crew. Mmoh, whose father was a professional tennis player from Nigeria, came to the Washington suburbs from Saudi Arabia and trains at Nick Bollettieri’s legendary boot camp.
These intensive training programs are not necessarily a straightforward solution to the problem of training the next generation. The U.S.T.A. academy has come under fire for seizing on young players too quickly and writing them off just as fast. A number of players who enrolled or trained there claim to have been let down or abandoned. Spencer Papa, an 18-year-old from Oklahoma, was 13 when he joined one of the first classes of boarders. Everyone who started when he did either quit early or was dropped. “I was the last one,” he says. “But last year, after I lost in the first round at Wimbledon, my coach got in touch and said it would probably be best if I started working with my dad.” (Papa’s father is a tennis instructor.) “If you don’t do really well by the time you’re 17, they just release you.” Another former student, Martin Redlicki, whose family moved from Chicago to Florida so he and his brother could train at the academy, agrees: “Some of the coaches still have the mentality from when they were playing, when Michael Chang was winning slams at 17.”

Jeremy Efferding, a leading junior who trained as a day student at the academy for six years beginning in 2005, describes the atmosphere as intense, adding: “You’re playing and doing fitness five hours a day, then doing school in between. The kids in the dorms are basically on lockdown.”
Efferding, who now plays for Texas A&M, says the academy’s biggest problem is its “one-size-fits-all mentality.” Jay Berger, the head of U.S.T.A. player development for men’s tennis, was a Top 10 ATP player 25 years ago and was known for his work ethic. “I remember Jay telling me that you should play so hard that somebody who’s never seen you play before should come up to you and say: ‘Dude, you have to stop right now. You’re going to hurt yourself,’ ” Efferding recalls. “I liked it, but I had a reputation for throwing up. He made me throw up all the time. I guarantee you Federer trains differently than Nadal. Agassi’s dad made him play for money as a little kid, and Sampras was a different cat entirely.”
Berger says the difficulties some players experienced led the academy to shift its focus away from their future professional success and toward their individual development (the desired result, of course, being a career in pro tennis). “The pressure was a little overwhelming,” he says. “But there’s a kind of training that you have to do to become really good at anything.” McEnroe is also quick to acknowledge the complaints: “We’ve made mistakes, and we’re learning. We want to help all American juniors. And we were wrong to think we could finalize a class when the boys are 14 and not allow the group to evolve.” Even so, McEnroe adds, “we haven’t had the same problems with the girls we took on at the same time.” He names several who are succeeding on the pro tour — Madison Keys, Sloane Stephens, Shelby Rogers — and says: “They’re actually ahead of schedule. I just think that’s interesting to note.”
McEnroe is encouraged by the potential of this group of young male players, though he notes a few bad habits. Kozlov, he says, “needs to clean up his forehand” — he has a tendency to hit the ball a bit flat. Tiafoe “is a little in and out,” meaning he sometimes loses focus on the court. Mmoh’s form can be erratic. “I never came into this role hoping that as an organization we could create a John McEnroe or a Pete Sampras,” McEnroe says, “but you can’t sit back and hope you’ll just stumble on one either.”
Rubin is one of
the few among his cohort who opted not to attend a tennis factory. Instead, he has remained at home in New York State, where he can play outdoors at best half the year. “People said I was crazy not to go, and it might have been fun, but what I had with my father and Lawrence always worked for me.”

Rubin’s father, Eric, who grew up playing tennis in Queens, was feeding balls to Noah as soon as he could walk. “Every day at 5 a.m., and usually during lunch hour and then after work,” Eric says. Kleger entered the picture when Noah was 7. “It was the best-taught job by a parent teaching his own kid,” Kleger recalls. “He didn’t yet have an advanced tactical sense, but his technique was already pretty good. He could hit a kick serve and a one-handed slice backhand.”
Rubin’s parents divorced when he was 14 and his sister was 19, and his tennis somehow became an object of the settlement.
“It wasn’t a carnival — let’s be honest,” Noah said of the divorce. The experience made him more independent, he said, and he threw himself into tennis — “this game I can control.” He went on: “No offense to anybody, but when I won that last point at Wimbledon, I felt very alone. It was a good feeling. I was playing for myself.”
The U.S.T.A. has provided financial assistance to Rubin at times — without which, his father says, he never would have been able to travel to national and international tournaments. But the U.S.T.A.’s involvement often came with complications. Two years ago, the organization flew Rubin to Paris for the junior French Open, but insisted on providing a coach, Nicholas Todero of the U.S.T.A., and limiting Rubin’s contact with Kleger.
“The deal was that I could go, but I couldn’t be on the court at his practices,” Kleger recalls. At Wimbledon that year, Kleger says that Rubin was upset “because they got on him for looking outside the court to his father and me. No offense to them, but their track record isn’t too great. I’ve known Patrick McEnroe­ since he was 12 years old. He’s a great kid. I respect him. He said, ‘Well, how would you feel if you were taking Noah to a tournament and we came over and told him how to play?’ My response was: ‘I’d say I’m grateful. I’m thankful. Are we playing that word game?’ ” (Kleger says the U.S.T.A. “has done a 180 since the beginning of the year” and now encourages players to retain their coaches even while training with the organization.)
Rubin has chosen an unusual path to success, and he himself is something of an outlier. Unlike his factory rivals — whose abundance of raw, god-given ability coaches work to mold into intelligent, polished playing — Rubin has shortcomings that are mostly innate. He possesses less natural athleticism than the best of his contemporaries do. (When he says “my greatest strength is my mental game,” it could be interpreted as an admission that he lacks a reliable weapon.) Plus, at 5-foot-9, he’s short. Professional tennis has changed over the past decade, an evolution often summed up as making the game more physical. To measure today’s player against one from a generation ago is to find someone more agile, brawnier and taller.
“I love the kid’s attitude,” McEnroe­ says of Rubin. “He has really good tennis I.Q. He’s extremely solid. The one thing missing, of course, is size. I mean, you look at the picture of him standing with Kozlov at Wimbledon, and Stefan’s only 16 but he’s a good two or three inches taller. And people say Stefan is short.”

Rios was an offensive genius who reached No. 1 in the world in 1998, largely by taking the ball on the rise and, Kleger says, “making players who hit with more pace uncomfortable, because he robbed you of time.” Both are 5-foot-9. “Now, whether there’s room for someone like that in 10 years, who knows?”
A few weeks
after Wimbledon, Rubin was on the distinctly unglamorous Futures circuit, where he and most of his peers will most likely spend the first several years of adulthood. The competition was in Godfrey, Ill. — “the kind of tournament almost designed to make you ask yourself if you really want to be doing this,” he said. It was held on the campus of a local community college, where the tennis pavilion had no locker room, just a single men’s room for players and officials to share. The total payout — for those competitors who weren’t playing N.C.A.A. tennis during the school year or didn’t plan to — was just $10,000, with prizes ranging from $117.50 for each first-round loser in men’s singles to the champion’s purse of $1,300.
To save on expenses, Rubin’s first-round opponent, Spencer Papa, was staying in the spare bedroom of local tennis boosters, whose teenage children were on hand to ferry him and another player to Walmart to stock up on Pedialyte. Rubin’s airfare and motel expenses were covered by the John McEnroe Tennis Academy on Randalls Island, which sent a traveling coach, Mark Bowtell, to keep him company.
Rubin’s success over the summer had put a target on his back. “Everyone wants to take a stab at him,” Bowtell said, adding that Rubin told him, “Now when someone beats me, they’ve beaten a Wimbledon champion.” Rubin got off to an easy start but fell apart. He won the first set 6-2, led the second 4-0 but lost it 7-5, and then dropped the final set 6-1. Papa said Rubin seemed to ease up just as he was about to walk away with the match. “I was mentally kind of down,” Papa told me, “but I had a lucky game when I held serve at 3-4, even though he was hitting good returns.” After that, Rubin tensed up. “He stopped coming forward on the baseline the way he normally does. I couldn’t tell what happened to him.” Papa added: “Even from the outset, he seemed like he was carrying himself differently, probably because of Wimbledon. We’re pretty good friends, and he’s always been a confident guy, but — well, I’d just say that everybody in the tournament came up to me after and said, ‘I’m so glad you beat him.’ ” (Eric Rubin says the reason his son lost was that he came down with a virus.)
Rubin was back at Randalls Island a few days later to hit with a college player whom Kleger had lined up. Kleger mentioned that he was also trying to arrange a practice date with Ivan Dodig, a visiting Croatian ATP player. Eric Rubin, who paced the perimeter of the court, occasionally called out to Kleger to pay attention to something, like the way his son was letting his racket droop slightly between shots. “It was O.K., but it was kind of funky,” Eric said. “It almost went back to ‘I’m 12 years old.’ ”
Rubin devoted nearly an hour to a drill that had him volleying at the net until his practice partner would send a deep topspin lob over his head. He ran down most of them at the baseline, skidding and leaning into the bounce like a squash player to flick a hard return shot from his shoelaces, with his back still facing the net. When a lob finally came up short, Rubin’s legs slackened and he stepped slowly toward the ball to put it away with an overhead smash. He pointed his racket toward the young man across the net and smiled gratefully. Even he didn’t mind having something come easily once in a while.

Two teenagers each reached the semifinals of tournaments this week, crashing parties that have been restricted to much older crowds in recent years.
One of them, Alexander Zverev, 17, was playing in the ATP 500-level tournament on the clay of his hometown, Hamburg, Germany. The other, Ana Konjuh, 16, was competing on hardcourts at a WTA International-level event in Istanbul.
Zverev’s accomplishment was the more stunning of the two: Teenage success stories have been far scarcer in the men’s game. Although Zverev lost to the top seed, David Ferrer, 6-0, 6-1, in his semifinal on Saturday, he hit several milestones in his four victories in the main draw of the tournament.
Zverev was the first 17-year-old to beat a top-20 player — No. 19 Mikhail Youzhny, whom he faced in the second round — since Richard Gasquet in 2004 and the first to reach an ATP semifinal at that age since Marin Cilic in 2006. Among active players, only the former No. 1s Rafael Nadal and Lleyton Hewitt reached ATP semifinals at a younger age.
Zverev, a top-ranked junior who won the boys’ title at the Australian Open in January, has found success at the professional level suddenly. He was ranked outside the top 800 at the beginning of this year and 665th at the beginning of the month. But after winning a tournament in Braunschweig, Germany, one of the largest on the Challenger circuit, and reaching the semifinals in Hamburg, he will have risen more than 500 spots in three weeks, to No. 160.
Zverev has joked that he was “born with a tennis racket in my hands.” His parents, Alexander and Irina, were successful tennis players for the Soviet Union, and his brother Mischa, 26, reached the top 50 in 2009. But the younger Alexander Zverev was already beating his brother in some practice games three years ago, when he was 14.
“I act like I’m angry, but I’m very proud of him and happy,” Mischa Zverev said of those losses.
Mischa Zverev gave his brother, nicknamed Sascha, advice before each match in Hamburg, having previously faced all the opponents Alexander Zverev faced there.
The increasing physicality of tennis has often been cited as the reason young players have not been able to break through as frequently in recent years, and Zverev is still growing comfortable with his long, growing limbs. But he has managed to succeed before reaching full physical maturity.
“Well, maybe I just proved those people wrong,” he said by telephone from Hamburg after his loss Saturday. “I don’t know. I tried to prove them wrong. The game got so much more physical, and I think the game got so much better than it was 20 years ago. That I got through to the semifinals in this tournament, this home tournament for me, I’m just really, really thankful and really happy.”
The German news media, eager for a Grand Slam champion, has embraced Zverev, with one headline calling him “the next Boris Becker.”
Zverev said that comparison was “a little too big at the moment,” adding that he would be happy with a career anywhere near as successful as Becker’s.

Since 2006, over 70,000 deaths in Mexico have been directly attributed to the illegal drug trade. This is likely an extreme underestimate due to huge numbers of deaths left unreported. While the statistics might seem surprising, these types of numbers are typical for many Latin American countries. The demand for illicit drugs from the United States has turned previously peaceful cities and nations into war-torn wastelands. While Latin America is suffering most of the consequences, the United States has its share of problems. Over 51 billion dollars of taxpayer money is spent yearly on the drug war. Is this really accomplishing anything? Other than incarcerating over 1.55 million nonviolent Americans every year who weren’t harming anyone but themselves? Drug arrests have contributed to the United States having the highest incarceration rate in the world.
As reported by Richard Viguerie
with The New York Times, The United States’ prison system costs over 50 billion per year — up 450 percent since 1985.
The drug war is failing for the same reason that prohibition did in the 1920s. Supply for alcohol was cut, while the demand still existed. This gave power to criminals who were willing to break the law to supply alcohol and make quick money. This is more true now than it was in the 1920s. Due to a more globalized economy, better established and more easily accessible trade routes, smuggling drugs into the country is easier than ever for cartels. The flawed logic here is that the drug war is something that can be won: If enough shipments are confiscated, or enough dealers are busted, the supply will end and drug abuse will cease to exist. Even if tomorrow, the head of the largest cartel were taken into custody, it wouldn’t make any difference. As long as demand exists from the United States for illegal drugs, there will always be someone willing to supply it.
After four decades, many Americans are wondering if it’s time for a change in policy. Drug usage rates have hovered around 8 to 9 percent since the 1970s, and accessibility to them is more common than ever. We have 42 years of proof that shows this approach doesn’t work, and I think it’s time for a different strategy. I believe the United States should follow the example of Portugal by decriminalizing possession of all drugs, and treating addiction as a health issue instead of a criminal one. Maia Szalavitz with Time reports that post-decriminalization, Portugal saw across-the-board drops in drug use. ’s powerful business dynasties.

JERUSALEM — As Israel began to redeploy significant numbers of its troops away from populated areas of Gaza on Sunday, an Israeli Air Force missile struck near the entrance of a United Nations school sheltering displaced Palestinians in Rafah, killing 10 people and wounding 35 others and drawing a new round of international condemnation.
The growing civilian death toll has stirred outrage in Europe and large parts of the Arab world and, combined with Sunday’s strike near the Rafah school, prompted Secretary General Ban Ki-moon of the United Nations to call the attack a “moral outrage and a criminal act” and to demand that those responsible for the “gross violation of international humanitarian law” be held accountable.
The State Department also condemned in harsh terms what it called “today’s disgraceful shelling” outside the school in Rafah. Witnesses near the school, where about 3,000 Palestinians had sought shelter, said that those killed or hurt were waiting in line for food supplies when a missile hit. A State Department spokeswoman, Jen Psaki, said that “the suspicion that militants are operating nearby does not justify strikes that put at risk the lives of so many innocent civilians.”
The Israeli Army said that it had targeted with the missile three members of Islamic Jihad on a motorcycle near the school, not the school itself, and was investigating a possible secondary explosion when the motorcycle was hit.
Even as Israel moved unilaterally to reduce military contact with Palestinians on the ground in Gaza, while waiting to see how the militant groups Hamas and Islamic Jihad would respond, it continued to fight around Rafah, near the border with Egypt. On Sunday, 71 Palestinians died, raising the total to 1,822, with 9,370 injured, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Estimates of the number of Palestinian combatants killed varied widely, with some Israeli officials suggesting that number was more than 700. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said Saturday that of the 1,525 dead Palestinians to that point, “at least 1,033 are civilians, of whom 329 are children and 187 are women.”
On the Israeli side, 64 soldiers and three civilians have died. Israeli officials confirmed Sunday that one of the fallen soldiers was a relative of Defense Minister Moshe Yaalon.
With its stated task of destroying Hamas’s tunnel network into Israel within days of being finished, Israel seemed to be trying to de-escalate the war without negotiating with Hamas, much as it did at the end of the last major Gaza operation, in 2009, when Israel declared a unilateral cease-fire. Large numbers of Israeli troops were moving to positions just inside Gaza, while others were redeploying to Israel.
Early Monday, the Israel Defense Forces announced a “temporary humanitarian window,” or cease-fire, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., though it said it did not apply to areas where soldiers are “currently operating,” like Rafah.

Peter Lerner, an Israeli Army spokesman, said that there were “substantial redeployments of the troops on the ground who will be regrouping, receiving further orders.” Some forces were still operating inside Gaza, especially around Rafah, he said, and the air force was continuing to bomb Gaza.
“It’s changing gears, but it’s still ongoing,” he said. Israel has never said precisely how many troops are operating in Gaza, only that there are “thousands.”
Mohammed Muafai, who works for the United Nations, said that he was inside the school when the missile hit. In a telephone interview, he said there were bodies on the ground, including two guards and a sanitation worker. He said seven more people from displaced families also died, including one selling flavored ice.
Last Wednesday, 21 Palestinians who sought refuge in a school run by the United Nations in the Jabaliya refugee camp
were killed

killed 16

Earlier on Sunday, airstrikes killed at least 30 Palestinians, medics and witnesses said.
Ashraf al-Qedra, a spokesman for the Palestinian Health Ministry, said that nine members of a family were killed in an air attack in Rafah. Earlier Sunday, six Palestinians were killed in separate airstrikes on houses in the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Israel said that 55 rockets were fired from Gaza on Sunday, and that its troops killed eight Hamas fighters in southern Gaza.
Israeli officials on Sunday defended their decision to announce the death of a missing Israeli soldier at 2 a.m., only hours after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu went on national television to say that he had no new information about the case.
Army spokesmen said Sunday that
the declaration of the death
of the soldier, Second Lt. Hadar Goldin, 23, was made as soon as possible and that DNA tests had been carried out on partial remains. The lieutenant and two colleagues were attacked by a Hamas squad that emerged from a tunnel on Friday, the army said. One of the Hamas fighters had exploded a suicide belt.
“We can’t determine if he was killed on the ground or from the blast,” said Colonel Lerner, the army spokesman. “The indications on the ground are that he was killed in the initial attack.”
He said that the tests had been carried out during the Sabbath because it was an emergency. The relatives of Lieutenant Goldin had made emotional appeals earlier on Saturday, before Mr. Netanyahu spoke, that Israel and its army not leave the lieutenant behind, and they said that they believed he was still alive.
The family buried him on Sunday in an emotional funeral attended by thousands at the military cemetery in Kfar Saba, near Tel Aviv.

On the cover of her new album, “The Future’s Void,” the South Dakota-raised noise-rocker EMA sports an Oculus Rift virtual reality headset, but the photograph was shot before that company’s recent $2 billion purchase by Facebook. And she wrote the song “
Satellites
,” which rages against government surveillance, months before the National Security Agency scandal broke.
“It’s freaking me out,” said EMA, whose real name is Erika M. Anderson. “I don’t know how this happened. I was writing about what I felt like writing about that year, but I felt out of touch. I was being kind of solitary and wasn’t really on the Internet. And now it’s all, like, almost too topical.”
Her obsession with science and technology courses through “The Future’s Void,” which is out on Tuesday on Matador Records. In its distorted guitars and hypnotic swirls of feedback, the record nods to her past work with the drone-rock band Gowns and her assertive debut solo album, “Past Life Martyred Saints,” which was lauded in many year-end lists in 2011. However, this time around, EMA, who plays multiple instruments and records alone in her home, also dives ambitiously into other genres, growling like Courtney Love in a critique of female objectification (“
So Blonde
”) and confessing her insecurities with new frailty atop somber electronic balladry (“
3Jane
”).
Ahead of her national and European tours, including shows on April 25 at Mercury Lounge and May 9 at Rough Trade in Brooklyn, the amusingly candid singer called from her home in Portland to talk with Stacey Anderson (no relation) about growing up a tomboy and meeting the metal star Glenn Danzig. These are excerpts from the conversation.
Q. What was it like to be a girl in the South Dakota hardcore scene?
A.
I was the only girl to front a band. Being around so many tough boys made me have to be really tough. I get obsessed with the idea of the void because, in some ways, that’s what South Dakota felt like. I used to think growing up there put me at a disadvantage because I didn’t have access to a lot of art, but I keep re-evaluating my relationship to it. Being totally free on those gravel roads with my friends and good music was the most awesome thing.
South Dakota has a strong gun culture, doesn’t it?
Yeah, I took a hunter safety class at 14 at the behest of my father. He’s an environmentalist Democrat hunter, which isn’t as rare as it seems, and he had this idea that maybe we could hunt together. I rolled up there with my shaved head and weird combat boots, and there’s a woman in there talking about the mark of the beast, how they want people to get chips put in their arms. I’m like, “Oh, you’re about to get a gun license. That’s amazing.”
“So Blonde” is a blast against stereotypes that blonde women face.
“So Blonde” is supposed to be kind of funny and meta-grunge. There’s a slight Kurt and Courtney reference. It’s also about my ambivalence of having that woman be the rock ’n’ roll role model. What do you do when the world only gives you one successful rocker-poet woman in your life, and that woman happens to be Courtney Love? I spent too many years being a Courtney apologist, and that wears you out.
Is the riot grrrl influence in that song “So Blonde” an effect of moving to the Pacific Northwest?
Those boys I hung out with used to call me “riot grrrl” in a way that I don’t know was totally complimentary. It came back now because one thing I really wanted to do on this record, something I’d been missing in music, is this idea of feminine grotesque, a voice that is just gnarly.
There’s
a picture
of Glenn Danzig and you as a teenager floating around the Internet and he’s actually smiling. What did you say to crack that serious facade of his?
I don’t remember. I don’t know. I just must have been my charming, cornfed self.

‘Antarctica: A Year on Ice’
(PG, 1:32) The extremes of Anthony Powell’s documentary might seem routine to fans of nature films, but the director, a photographer, produces some dazzling imagery in his droll tour of Antarctica’s scientific stations and their long-term residents. (Nicolas Rapold)
★ ‘The Babadook’
(No rating, 1:35) Jennifer Kent’s feature debut is a deceptively simple, effectively scary tale of a storybook demon that comes to life and torments a young mother and her 6-year-old son. It’s a minor masterpiece of the psychological horror genre. (A. O. Scott)
★ ‘Beyond the Lights’
(PG-13, 1:56) A swooning, touching romance — and occasionally silly, but none the worse for that — about a pop star (Gugu Mbatha-Raw) who falls for the police officer (Nate Parker) who saves her life. Written and directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, the movie is canny about celebrity, smart about feminism and also unafraid to embrace melodrama. It also features Minnie Driver as one of the modern screen’s scariest stage mothers. (Scott)
‘Big Hero 6’
(PG, 1:45) This bright, visually sumptuous computer-animated feature from Walt Disney Studios is a superhero movie with a story from a Marvel comic book, if one rendered with the wit and texture often associated with Pixar. Set in the future, it turns on a geeky 14-year-old orphaned boy, a beautiful, bouncy robot and a Scooby Doo-like posse, who face down a villain and, ta-da, save the day. (Manohla Dargis)
★ ‘Birdman’
(R, 1:59) This funny, frenetic, rambunctiously showboating entertainment from the director Alejandro G. Iñárritu (
“Babel”
) stars a blissed-out Michael Keaton as a Hollywood has-been turned Broadway second-chancer who’s about to open a play based on the Raymond Carver story “What We Talk About When We Talk About Love.” The crack supporting cast includes Zach Galifianakis, Edward Norton, Andrea Riseborough, Amy Ryan, Emma Stone, Naomi Watts and Lindsay Duncan. (Dargis)
★ ‘Boyhood’
(R, 2:45) Radical in its conceit, familiar in its everyday details, Richard Linklater’s masterpiece follows a boy, Mason (Ellar Coltrane), who’s 6 when the story opens and 18 when it ends. In between, he goes to school; argues with his sister, Samantha (Lorelei Linklater, the director’s daughter); and watches his mother, Olivia (Patricia Arquette), struggle with work and men, including her ex-husband, Mason Sr. (Ethan Hawke). Shot over 12 consecutive years, the film exists at the juncture of classical cinema and the modern art film without being slavishly indebted to either tradition. (Dargis)
★ ‘Citizenfour’
(R, 1:54) Laura Poitras’s documentary about Edward Snowden, the former National Security Agency contractor who revealed the startling extent of the United States government’s electronic surveillance activities, is a sharp and scary fable about the often invisible power of the modern state, and the vulnerability of individuals. (Scott)

(R, 1:48) Justin Simien’s ambitious and dazzling debut feature is a sharp satire of Obama-era race relations on the campus of an elite college, and a great deal more. ‘Dumb and Dumber To’
(PG-13, 1:49) Dumbier, not funnier. (Dargis)
‘Exodus: Gods and Kings’
(PG-13, 2:30) Ridley Scott’s attempt to bring a famous chunk of the Hebrew Bible to life, in 3-D no less, is crowded with well-known actors (Christian Bale, Joel Edgerton and others) and has the makings of a provocative study of power, rebellion and loyalty. (R, 1:58, in Swedish) This brilliant, viciously amusing takedown of bourgeois complacency, gender stereotypes and assumptions, and the illusion of security, rubs your face in human frailty as relentlessly as any Michael Haneke film. (Stephen Holden)
★ ‘Foxcatcher’
(R, 2:14) In this eerie horror story about one American have and one have-not, the director Bennett Miller revisits — with mixed results and superb performances — a catastrophically violent episode that upended the lives of the heir John Eleuthère du Pont (Steve Carell), and the Olympic wrestler Mark Schultz (Channing Tatum). ‘A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night’
(No rating, 1:47, in Farsi) By the time the vampire in the chador is skateboarding down a dark, desolate street, the director Ana Lily Amirpour has ensured that her debut feature will roll on in your memory. ‘Gone Girl’
(R, 2:25) At its strongest, David Fincher’s adaptation of the Gillian Flynn’s best seller — a woman (Rosamund Pike) has gone missing and her husband (a very good Ben Affleck) may be to blame — plays like a queasily, at times gleefully, funny horror movie about a modern marriage, one that’s partly disintegrated because of downward mobility and lost privilege. ‘The Lady Eve’
(Friday through Sunday) “It isn’t often that this corner has good reason to bang a gong and holler ‘Hurry, hurry, hurry!’ ” So hollered the New York Times critic Bosley Crowther in 1941 in support of Preston Sturges and his effervescent and deeply sexy screwball comedy, which features Henry Fonda and Barbara Stanwyck at the top of their considerable powers. Sturges, who kept a markedly light tone on the set (he put Stanwyck at ease by wearing a bathrobe when he filmed her bedroom scene), was concerned that sneak preview audiences would snub the film’s numerous pratfalls. He needn’t have worried: Head over heels is the appropriate response, both for the film’s conniving characters and for its audience. Let There Be Light: The Films of John Huston
(Friday through Jan. 11) When the seemingly inimitable voice of John Huston came roaring back in

“The Treasure of the Sierra Madre,”

; $10. (Grode)

and “Alfred Hitchcock Presents.” All of this and
“Health,”
the 1980 political satire that Ronald Reagan called “the world’s worst movie.” Museum of Modern Art Roy and Niuta Titus Theaters, 212-708-9400,
moma.org
; $12. (Grode)

WASHINGTON — The State Department will delay its decision on construction of the Keystone XL pipeline until it has a clearer idea of how legal challenges to the pipeline’s route through Nebraska will be settled, State Department officials said Friday.
Both supporters and opponents of the pipeline criticized the delay as a political ploy aimed at punting the final call on the divisive project until after the midterm elections in November.
The 1,700-mile pipeline, which would carry crude oil from the Alberta oil sands in Canada to Gulf Coast refineries, has emerged as an issue in the battle for control of the Senate. Vulnerable Democratic incumbents from oil-rich states, like Senators Mary L. Landrieu of Louisiana, who is chairwoman of the Senate Energy Committee, and Mark Begich of Alaska, have urged President Obama to approve the pipeline.
But approving the pipeline before the election could staunch the flow of money from liberal donors and fund-raisers who oppose the project, like Tom Steyer, a California billionaire. Mr. Steyer, who has personally asked Mr. Obama to reject the pipeline, is positioned to play a major role in influencing the midterms: He has pledged to spend $100 million to support candidates who back strong policies to fight climate change.
Delaying the pipeline decision until after the election could help Democrats on both sides of the issue. Supporters could court voters by calling for its approval, while liberals who oppose the pipeline could still enjoy financial support from donors like Mr. Steyer.
“We’re seeing politics trumping policy making,” said Cindy Schild, a senior manager at the American Petroleum Institute, which represents oil companies’ interests in Washington.
The Senate Republican leader, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, said in

In one form or another,
Damien Echols
has now been a star of at least five films, but this is not a distinction that fills him with pride.
Along with Jason Baldwin and Jessie Misskelley Jr., Mr. Echols, now 39, was convicted in 1994 of
the murder of three boys
in West Memphis, Ark.
After years of efforts to prove their innocence, Mr. Echols, a onetime death-row inmate, Mr. Baldwin and Mr. Misskelley — who together came to be known as the West Memphis Three —
were freed
in 2011 in a deal that required them to plead guilty to the murders.
Regarded by their supporters as victims of a runaway prosecution, the men have been subjects of four documentaries: the three-part
“Paradise Lost”
series (1996-2011), directed by Joe Berlinger and Bruce Sinofsky, and
“West of Memphis”
(2012), directed by Amy Berg. And now their lives and the case are being depicted in a scripted dramatic feature,
“Devil’s Knot,”
due Friday from the director Atom Egoyan.
For Mr. Echols, the constant attention has a double edge: It helps keep attention on the crimes and efforts to exonerate him, but also forces him to revisit a traumatic experience.
“You have to keep talking about it,” he said in a recent interview, “but at the same time, I’ve reached a point where I’m so sick of this stuff. It’s eaten up 20 years of my life.”
Yet the creators of these movies find themselves entrenched in the projects more deeply than most typical filmmakers. They say the case is worth revisiting and revisiting, even after the cameras stop rolling. To them, their work is not finished until the murders are solved and justice is done.
“There’s no conclusive ending,” said Elizabeth Fowler, a producer of
“Devil’s Knot.”
“There are still things going on that are worthy of documentation.” Ms. Fowler, who optioned Mara Leveritt’s nonfiction book of the same title as the basis for the project, has pursued her own research into the case, communicating with families of the victims, lawyers for the defendants, private investigators and others.

All the filmmakers say they remain connected to the case to varying degrees, continuing to receive tips and information that they share with one another and research teams. Mr. Berlinger said that when he and Mr. Sinofsky first traveled to Arkansas in 1993 to make the original
“Paradise Lost”
for HBO, they expected to tell a story about “kids killing kids, and how teenagers became so disaffected from life that they became devil worshipers,” a theory advanced by prosecutors and media coverage.
Instead, Mr. Berlinger said, they realized “this was a film about wrongful conviction” and how “the town fell for the prejudice that prosecutors were selling.”
Though the documentary won Emmy and Peabody Awards, Mr. Berlinger said he and Mr. Sinofsky were frustrated that it did not help free the defendants. In 2000, they made a follow-up film whose goal, Mr. Berlinger said, “was just unabashed advocacy.”
The “Paradise Lost” movies helped inspire the creation of sites like
wm3.org
that support the West Memphis Three, and attract celebrity allies like Eddie Vedder and Johnny Depp, as well as the “Lord of the Rings” filmmakers Peter Jackson and Fran Walsh, who spent their own money to pursue further investigations of the crimes.

To the Editor:
Re “
Perpetuating Schizophrenia’s Stigma
” (Op-Ed, Aug. 13):
I salute Edward Larkin and Irene Hurford for demonstrating the disparities in psychiatric care between the haves and the have-nots, and especially for focusing on the plight of those with schizophrenia who fall through the cracks. However, differences between the old drugs and the new drugs are not as clear-cut as the writers suggest.
For example, my colleague Robert J. Hitzemann and I showed in several studies that when the old drug Haldol, which the writers said “can cause a multitude of serious side effects,” was used in very low doses, it produced the same effect on the dopamine receptors, the primary receptors implicated in schizophrenias, as the newer drugs, with many fewer side effects.
But it was frequently used in very much higher doses, which could account for the high incidence of tardive dyskinesia. This, together with aggressive marketing of the new drugs and the desire by clinicians to practice “cutting edge” medicine, led to drugs like Haldol falling into disrepute. So we may never know if ultralow doses of Haldol will be a cheap, safe and effective treatment for schizophrenia — unless, of course, in this era of cost containment, we revisit some of the old drugs to find out.
JACK HIRSCHOWITZ
New York, Aug. 13, 2014
The writer is a clinical professor of psychiatry at Mount Sinai School of Medicine.
To the Editor:
Edward Larkin and Irene Hurford are more correct than they may realize when they write that schizophrenia “is deeply misunderstood,” then inform us in their case example that “a diagnosis became clear: he had schizophrenia” and go on to describe an organic illness whose symptoms are to be treated by the “right” drug.
Despite decades of research, no organic marker or defect has been discovered that distinguishes people who receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia from control populations, and drugs, at best, mitigate symptoms, often with horrendous side effects.
The wisdom that, whatever the organic contribution, schizophrenia represents an unusual configuration of personality that arises from pathogenic childhood experiences and, at least in some instances, can be basically modified by an intensive psychoanalytically informed relationship has all but been lost.
In the past, some psychiatric hospitals supported such treatment, but now that medicine and psychiatry have been co-opted by the pharmaceutical industry, the treatment standard is symptom suppression and superficial social readjustment.
In the process, an important aspect of our humanism has been lost as well.
MICHAEL ROBBINS
Amherst, Mass., Aug. 13, 2014
The writer is a psychoanalyst and the author of “Experiences of Schizophrenia.”

At America Magazine today, there’s
a very long dialogue
between myself and Father James Martin of the Society of Jesus, the prolific author and commentator, that jumps off from my recent, perhaps-slightly-controversial
column
on Pope Francis and the situation within the Roman Catholic Church. I’m very grateful to Father Martin and the editors at America for putting the conversation together, and hopefully our dialogue will be interesting to readers, even if we did not exactly resolve every intra-Catholic division across our 6,000-odd words of back and forth.
Naturally, reading it over in the cold light of hindsight, all sorts of further points occur to me, but I’ll just throw out one meta-observation for now. One of the interesting and challenging things about intra-Catholic conflict and disputation is that it takes place across multiple (and very different) realms: It happens within the actual structure of the church, in the (prayerful and pious, of course) contests for ecclesiastical influence; it happens in the wider secular arena, in mass media and mass culture and wherever the church is covered, debated, depicted or attacked; and then it happens within those Catholic institutions (educational and medical and cultural and charitable) that are partially tied to the structure of the church but answer to secular pressures and sometimes serve secular masters as well. And one of the things that’s very clear when you move back and forth between different spheres and different perspectives on Catholicism is that this multiplicity makes it possible for just about every group within the church’s fold to feel beleaguered, ill-used and dispossessed.
Thus from the perspective of many progressive Catholics, the John Paul II and Benedict eras are seen as periods when they were effectively silenced, or at least marginalized, within the formal structure of the church, and when they were expected (as Father Martin suggests, inviting me to greater sympathy for the progressive perspective) to effectively keep their heads down and keep their real opinions to themselves. But then from the perspective of more conservative or traditional Catholics, the fact that some priests or bishops or religious felt constrained in their statements and criticisms is almost beside the point, because their perspective had a kind of permanent soapbox in just about every major newspaper and magazine and television network and educational setting (many officially Catholic settings included), where the correctness of the progressive perspective was taken for granted, and the supposed rigid reactionary dogmatism of the pontiffs was perpetually sneered at, critiqued or just dismissed — whether by prominent liberal Catholics, prominent lapsed or collapsed Catholics, or just by the many, many people who felt qualified to take a dig at the pope.
So as the ground within the institutional church has shifted, at least a little, under Pope Francis, there’s been a palpable sense among progressive Catholics that after being a loyal opposition for so many years, it’s only fair to ask conservative Catholics to chin up and show a little more loyalty in their turn. But to this ask, the conservatives are inclined to retort (when they don’t accuse liberals of misreading the pontiff, which is still the more common move) that they’ve
already
been taking it on the chin for decades, thank you very much, and not only from the culture writ large, but in arguments with media-journalistic-academic Catholics who can seem, at times, anything but loyal.
And the reality is that because all the different spheres of contention clearly matter to the future of the faith, both sides have an understandable perspective on the situation. This is not, unfortunately, a commonality that obviously lends itself to achieving common ground. (It’s not as if there are obvious bargains to be made:
We’ll trade you seven episcopal appointments and a cardinal’s hat for a larger orthodox presence in
the Catholic Theological Association
and veto power over how the network news and Buzzfeed cover intra-church debates …
) But at the very least it’s helpful to recognize how others see the world: Conservative Catholics can profit from remembering that, yes, they have exercised real institutional power and imposed real litmus tests within the church these last forty years, and whatever that power’s limits they aren’t
just
beleaguered and beset, while their progressive co-religionists can profit from recognizing that while the ecclesiastical levers have often been out of their reach, their cause still has potent forces behind it, real powers in its corner, whose exertions and influence matter immensely to the shape of the church’s internal conflicts … if not necessarily to their ultimate resolution.

Ralph Fasanella’s painting “Subway Riders” has not budged since 1995, when it became the first oil painting to be installed in a New York City subway station. Now it is heading out on the road.
On Tuesday morning the painting was removed from its display case across from the token booth at the 53rd Street and Fifth Avenue station (E and M trains) so deftly that people in the thin stream of passers-by heading for the turnstiles did not even turn to look. It was then carted off to form part of a traveling exhibition,
“Self Taught Genius: Treasures From the American Folk Art Museum.”
The show, which includes 110 works from the museum’s permanent collection, opens in Manhattan on Tuesday. Then, embarking on a three-and-a-half-year journey, it will make its way to a half-dozen cities, from San Diego to Tampa, before returning to the subway station. Although the museum owns more than 100 works by Mr. Fasanella, a painter who specialized in streetscapes and working-class life, it zeroed in on “Subway Riders” for “Self-Taught Genius.”
“This is momentous,” said Stacy C. Hollander, the museum’s chief curator. “This is one of the most significant paintings in our collection, and we’ve never been able to show it in the museum.”
“Subway Riders,” painted in 1950, depicts a scene familiar to New Yorkers: six tired riders, seated hip-to-hip, and two standees, all lost in their private worlds. “We don’t know the people sitting next to us, but in a way we do,” Mr. Fasanella said when his painting was first installed. “We are with them every day. The woman in the flowered hat: She’s an Irish schoolteacher. The black man reading the newspaper, the Puerto Rican woman with the baby — I know I know them. The worker slumped in his seat with his eyes closed, is that me?”
This year, the centennial of Mr. Fasanella’s birth, is shaping up to be a big one for the artist, who died in 1997. Nearly 20 of his paintings are on display at the
Smithsonian American Art Museum
, where “Ralph Fasanella: Lest We Forget” opened on Friday and will come to the Folk Art Museum in Manhattan in September. He also has shows at A.F.L.-C.I.O. headquarters in Washington and at the
Fenimore Art Museum in Cooperstown, N.Y.
Mr. Fasanella grew up on Sullivan Street in Greenwich Village, where his father hauled ice for a living. He served with the
Lincoln Brigade
of American volunteers who fought fascism during the Spanish Civil War and, after returning to the United States, he worked as a union organizer.
In 1944, bothered by pain in his right hand, he began drawing and painting as self-administered physical therapy. Within a few years he had attracted enough attention to be included in a group show with Philip Evergood, Jacob Lawrence and Ben Shahn at the ACA Gallery in Manhattan.
While riding the subway from his apartment on the Upper West Side to his job as a machinist in Long Island City, Queens, he began sketching fellow passengers with a marking pen on the classified-ad pages of The New York Times. From these drawings, “Subway Riders” evolved.
In the 1980s, Ron Carver, a retired union organizer and admirer of Mr. Fasanella’s art (he is the curator of the
A.F.L.-C.I.O. exhibition
), created a nonprofit organization, Public Domain, to acquire Mr. Fasanella’s paintings and place them in public buildings. He and Mr. Fasanella offered to donate the painting to the museum on the condition that it be put on permanent display in the subway through the Arts for Transit and Urban Design program.
“I want to see art about working people in the places they frequent,” Mr. Fasanella said. “I’d rather have people see this painting in the subway than any museum.”

A woman who died of an apparent heart attack at a New York City hair salon on Tuesday will be tested for the Ebola virus out of “an abundance of caution” because she had recently been in West Africa, city health officials said.
The woman, whose name was not released, came to the United States 18 days earlier from one of the four West African countries most affected by the Ebola outbreak, the health department said. She did not show symptoms of the virus before her death.
Health officials said they were testing the woman’s remains because she had a travel history within the 21-day incubation period for the virus. Test results were expected early Wednesday.
The city has been
tracking about 300 people
who had traveled in West Africa. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention gives the city a daily list of travelers coming to New York City from those countries.
Fire Department officials said they were called to the hair salon, African Queen Hair Braiding, at 32 Belmont Avenue in Brooklyn, around 2:30 p.m. Tuesday for a patient in cardiac arrest. The woman was pronounced dead there, fire officials said.
A hazmat unit responded, along with officials from the medical examiner’s office, the health department and the Police Department, said Jim Long, a Fire Department spokesman. The medical examiner’s office collected blood specimens from the woman and gave them to the health department for testing, he said.
On Tuesday night, three responders who entered the store wearing protective suits were being cleaned, according to the department’s decontamination protocols, Mr. Long said. Two others who helped with that process were also being cleaned, Mr. Long said.
“You have a well-traveled area of Brooklyn with a beauty salon that is well-traveled, and we’re taking precautionary steps that if, in fact, this turns out to be a positive case, that we’re in front of it,” Mr. Long said.
The police blocked off the commercial area to the public on Tuesday night. Emergency vehicles were gathered and floodlights lighted the street. At least one responder was seen wearing a hazmat suit as he walked out of a building.
Five airports in the United States, including Kennedy International Airport in New York and Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, have been screening passengers arriving from Liberia, Sierra Leone, Mali and Guinea. These travelers are monitored for 21 days and checked twice daily for temperatures and symptoms, according to guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Dr. Craig Spencer, a New Yorker who had Ebola,
was released
from Bellevue Hospital Center last week after recovering from the virus.

A day after State Senator John L. Sampson survived a heated primary in Brooklyn, one of his former consultants was convicted on federal corruption charges of conspiring with Mr. Sampson to steal $100,000 from the New York Democratic Senate Campaign Committee in an invoicing scheme.
After a one-week trial, a federal jury found the consultant, Melvin E. Lowe, guilty of conspiracy and wire fraud. He was also convicted of subscribing to false tax returns, failing to file tax returns and causing a bank employee to make a false report.
Mr. Lowe, 53, of Manhattan, remained free on bail after appearing in federal court in White Plains on Wednesday in front of Judge Vincent L. Briccetti. His court-appointed lawyer, Theodore S. Green, said in a telephone interview that his client planned to appeal. Mr. Lowe’s sentencing was set for Dec. 19.
In a statement on Wednesday, Preet Bharara, the United States attorney in Manhattan, said Mr. Lowe’s conviction would help to restore public confidence in New York State politics.
“As the jury found, Lowe participated in a series of back-room deals in which the bridge of corruption extended between the world of elected officials and their complicit consultants,” he said. “Consultants, like elected officials, need to be held accountable in order to clean up our political system.”
The verdict arrived as
Mr. Sampson celebrated winning his primary
in Brooklyn, despite the cloud of a federal indictment in an unrelated case and endorsements of his three rivals by prominent Democrats like Mayor Bill de Blasio and Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo.
Mr. Sampson, who has not been charged in this case, is under federal indictment on charges that he lied about his ownership of a liquor store and embezzled more than $400,000 from the sale of foreclosed homes.

Mr. Lowe, who was arrested in October, was convicted on all of the nine charges brought against him in a criminal complaint. Perry A. Carbone and James McMahon prosecuted the case.
According to the United States attorney’s news release, Mr. Lowe was hired as a consultant by the campaign committee after Democrats took control of the State Senate in 2009 and Mr. Sampson was appointed the leader of his party’s conference. At Mr. Sampson’s request in 2010, he arranged for a New Jersey-based consultant to bill the committee for $100,000 in printing services that were not performed, the news release said.
Mr. Lowe allowed the consultant to keep $5,000 and he gave $20,000 to Michael Nieves, a political operative based in Queens, who had helped the Democrats regain power. He kept the remaining $75,000 for his own firm, which he used to renovate his second home in Georgia.
Mr. Lowe was also convicted on charges that he failed to report more than $2.1 million in consulting income from 2007 to 2012. He filed tax returns for 2007 through 2009 in 2010 and reported less than $25,000 in income for each year. He did not file returns for the years 2010, 2011 and 2012.
The release also said Mr. Lowe caused an assistant manager at his bank to make a false report to his mortgage lender, reporting $80,000 in his checking account when it contained only $2,156.
The conviction stemmed from an investigation that has already felled Shirley L. Huntley, a former Democratic state senator from Queens. She was sentenced to a year and a day in prison after she pleaded guilty to stealing taxpayers’ money through a nonprofit organization she was running.
Malcolm A. Smith, a Democratic state senator from Queens who was seeking re-election but lost his primary on Tuesday, is awaiting a retrial on bribery charges that grew out of the inquiry. A judge granted a mistrial in June.

BLETCHLEY, England —  When “Captain Ridley’s shooting party” gathered here in late August 1938 as weekend guests at Bletchley Park, a Buckinghamshire country house,  they were accompanied by one of the finest chefs from the Savoy hotel. But the hunting that took place wasn’t the usual. The visitors were members of MI6 and the Government Code and Cypher School in Britain, scouting out a retreat for code breakers who would be needed in the coming war.
By now, of course, the estate’s cover is fully blown. This
mock-Tudor, mock-Gothic, red brick mansion
, framed by aged trees and with a picturesque pond, has become familiar from documentaries and television broadcasts and will soon become even more well known from the new film “
The Imitation Game
.”
Perhaps a hundred yards away, the bucolic landscaping comes to an end, with prefab-looking buildings crammed together and labeled things like “Hut 6” or “Hut 8.” Here, in drab rooms, about 9,000 mathematicians, linguists, cryptographers, clerks and classicists worked around the clock throughout the war to break German codes.
But for three decades after the war, who knew? Britain’s Official Secrets Act erased the history and silenced the participants. The estate, about an hour by train northwest of London, became a training school for teachers and then for postal workers. In 1991, there were plans to demolish it for a housing development.
But that was without reckoning with the growing understanding of what had happened here. Code breaking helped the Allies plan D-Day, turned the tide on the Russian front and helped foil U-boat attacks in the Atlantic. Churchill famously called the workers here geese who “laid the golden eggs and never cackled.” So when the Bletchley Park Trust was established and opened a museum here in 1993, the point was to show off some golden eggs, and perhaps even cackle a bit.
The museum
was also tapping into interest in Alan Turing: the brilliant mathematician, master code breaker and irascible, persecuted genius of “The Imitation Game.” Turing and Bletchley Park have inspired another feature film (“Enigma”), a play (“Breaking the Code”), television series (“Codebreakers,” “The Bletchley Circle”) and a growing library of books, most notably the extraordinary 1983 biography by Andrew Hodges, “Alan Turing: The Enigma” (which provides very loose inspiration for the new movie).

Bletchley Park displays a signed copy of Prime Minister Gordon Brown’s 2009 government apology. (Turing received
a posthumous royal pardon in 2013
.)
And while Bletchley Park has not had an easy time of it — in 2008, a hundred academics signed
a letter to The Times of London
, outraged by disrepair and neglect here — a recent visit showed it to be exceptionally vigorous. After receiving a $7.9 million government grant and raising $4.7 million from other sources, Bletchley Park completed the
first stage of a planned renovation
in June, restoring buildings and landscaping, creating a visitor center with an introductory exhibition and mounting new exhibitions in the “huts.”
Continue reading the main story
Now, with “The Imitation Game” poised to increase attention further (though its account of Turing’s code breaking is startlingly jumbled), Bletchley Park has opened a
yearlong exhibition about the making of the film
as a lure for “set-jetters” eager to visit where parts were filmed.
The other exhibitions here strike a more sober and weighty note,  though with  some flaws: They are splintered among many buildings; there is no systematic narrative; older exhibitions mix with the new. The effect is a little like that of the mansion, where rooms were added in different eras and with different styles.
But, in the end, it doesn’t matter: There is more here than can be absorbed in a single visit.
An exhibition about Turing
presents a survey of his mathematical papers, along with personal artifacts (including his teddy bear, in front of which he might have practiced his mathematics lectures at Cambridge University).
Another exhibition sketches the daily life of this secluded wartime world, with its high concentrations of women, as well as eccentric geniuses like the classicist Alfred Dillwyn Knox (who had famously pieced together papyrus fragments found in an Egyptian cave). Ian Fleming also spent time here.
Displays of
German coding machines
show just how daunting a task the code breakers faced: Those machines contained rotating discs and a plug board that, on the German Navy’s Enigma, for example, allowed for about a billion million million possibilities — and settings were changed every day.
In the huts, sound and video installations evoke the frantic yet meticulous work that went on. Turing’s office, in Hut 8, looks as if he had just stepped out, his cryptic markings covering a blackboard. Desks throughout the complex, like his, are covered with pencils, pads, typewriters and reference volumes — state of the era’s cryptographic art. Nearby are higher-tech touch screens that guide us through some techniques that were used.
These exhibitions are likely to grow in importance over time, because they are so detailed and careful — good correctives for growing misconceptions. For example, the most common image now associated with Bletchley Park is of
the Bombe
, a magnificent machine whose clicking rotors are also often used in “The Imitation Game” as evidence of Turing’s genius. The Bombes were all dismantled after the war, but in 2007, a working model was recreated that now hypnotically draws visitors to a demonstration.
But however impressive, the Bombe is, so to speak, overblown. It is not, the exhibition reminds us, a computer. It does no calculations. It simply runs through possible Enigma settings. Polish cryptographers had built a simpler one before the war. The Bombe was necessary, but insufficient.
The real advances in computer technology occurred in a roomsize monstrosity with over 1,500 vacuum tubes, built by an engineer,
Tommy Flowers
, and known as the Colossus. It may have been the world’s first programmable electronic computer, and was used to break another notoriously complex code, one used by Hitler and the German high command. It, too, was demolished, but a working reconstruction is the centerpiece of the independently run
National Museum of Computing,
located here in space rented from Bletchley Park (and well worth visiting).

Continue reading the main story
In many ways, too, the human decoding work was more impressive than the mechanical. Each day, the task was to determine the Enigma settings that were used. Possibilities had to be narrowed by statistical analysis and clever deductions before the Bombe could be used. And that was where Turing and his colleagues showed their brilliance.
A touch screen here gives a particularly elegant example. Every time a letter was encoded by an Enigma machine, the Enigma’s rotors would advance, changing the code settings for the following letter. So identical letters would rarely have identical codings, even within the same message. But the Enigma also had a crucial quirk: A letter could never be encoded as itself. (A W in code was never a W in the original.)
One day, a German dispatch seemed peculiar to
Mavis Batey, one of Bletchley’s leading code breakers
: It did not contain a single L. Batey guessed that it was a test message, that the operator, feeling lazy, sent it off by just hitting a single letter over and over. So this message was entirely composed of the one letter the coded text did not contain: L. This led her to the day’s Enigma setting. And that setting decoded other messages that led to the British Navy’s victory in the
1941 Battle of Matapan
, in Italy.
Is there another example in history when a battle was won because of a single letter?

SINTRA, Portugal — The European Central Bank was basically intended to do one thing: keep inflation in a cage. But its mission has turned out to be a lot more complicated than that.
That was the challenge facing an elite group of policy makers and economists gathered this week at a golf resort here outside Lisbon to brainstorm about how the central bank can combat the euro zone’s continuing economic problems with only a limited arsenal and a dwindling supply of ammunition.
The question has become more urgent in light of a growing recognition — acknowledged on Monday in perhaps the frankest terms yet by Mario Draghi, the bank’s president — that the euro zone is at risk of sliding into deflation, a downward price spiral that can ultimately destroy corporate profits and the ability of businesses to hire.
The deflation danger comes amid a credit crisis, a persistent banking problem and a citizenry angry at the slow pace of recovery, as gains by anti-euro political parties in
elections to the European Parliament
have vividly demonstrated.
Expectations run high that the central bank will take some sort of action when its governing council meets on June 5. The annual inflation rate, at 0.7 percent, remains well below the central bank’s target of close to 2 percent. But what the officials will do next week is still something of a mystery, and many economists question whether new measures would have any meaningful impact, given that the bank has already cut its benchmark interest rate close to zero.
Mr. Draghi said in unusually direct terms on Monday that there was a risk the euro zone could become caught in the trap of falling prices, a “classic deflationary cycle” that would require large-scale purchases of bonds or other assets to reverse. The statement may have been part of an attempt by Mr. Draghi to prepare the ground for controversial and exceptional measures.
“What we need to be particularly watchful for at the moment is the potential for a negative spiral to take hold between low inflation, falling inflation expectations and credit, in particular in stressed countries,” Mr. Draghi said in a speech that opened the two-day conference.
